title: Woe to Ariel: Lip Worship and a Sealed Book
summary: The LORD will besiege Ariel, the city where David camped, and bring her down to the dust, then suddenly scatter her enemies like chaff and a vanishing dream. Her people are spiritually blind, honoring God with their lips while their hearts are far away, and their leaders hide their plans from him as if the clay could outwit the potter. Yet a day is coming when the deaf will hear, the blind will see, the humble will rejoice, and Jacob will no longer be ashamed.
story: The second woe of this section (chapters 28 to 33) turns fully to Jerusalem. Chapter 28 exposed its leaders' false refuge; chapter 29 exposes the deeper problem beneath it, a religion of routine that no longer knows God. The chapter moves twice from judgment to hope: first from siege to sudden deliverance (verses 1 to 8), then from blindness and hypocrisy to a coming day of hearing and seeing (verses 9 to 24). Both movements anticipate what follows in the book: the actual siege and rescue of Jerusalem in chapters 36 and 37, and the promises of opened eyes and ears in chapters 32, 35, and 42.
historical:
Ariel is a name for Jerusalem, identified by the phrase "the city of Ariel where David camped" (verse 1), since David captured Jerusalem and made it his capital (2 Samuel 5:6-9). The siege described in verses 1 to 8 is usually connected with the Assyrian threat that culminated in Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC. In that year Assyria overran the fortified cities of Judah and threatened Jerusalem, but the city was not taken, and Isaiah 37:36 records that the angel of the LORD struck down the Assyrian army in a single night. Verses 5 to 8 read like a preview of that sudden reversal: the attackers who seem so solid vanish like a dream.

The second half of the chapter reflects the political atmosphere of Hezekiah's court, where officials were planning alliances in secret. Verse 15's woe on those who "dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD" probably refers to the negotiations with Egypt that chapters 30 and 31 condemn openly. Isaiah's complaint was not only that the plans were unwise, but that they were hidden from God and from his prophet.
cultural:
The name Ariel is a wordplay. Ezekiel 43:15-16 uses a very similar word for the hearth of the altar where sacrifices burned, and verse 2 says Jerusalem will be "like an altar hearth" before God, a place of fire and death. The name may also suggest the meaning lion of God. Verse 1's call to let the festivals recur year after year is bitter irony: the city keeps its religious calendar while its heart is elsewhere. Verse 4's voice "like a spirit from the ground" alludes to necromancy, the practice of consulting the dead through mediums, whose spirits were thought to whisper or chirp from the earth (compare 8:19).

The image of a sealed scroll (verses 11 and 12) comes from ancient documents. Important texts were rolled up, tied, and sealed with clay impressed by a seal, so that only an authorized person could open them. Many such clay seal impressions (called bullae) have been found in Jerusalem from the period of the Judean kings. Reading itself was a limited skill. Isaiah's point is that the literate and the illiterate alike are cut off from God's message: one says the book is sealed, the other says he cannot read. The potter, the most common craftsman of the ancient town, gives the image in verse 16: what would it mean for a pot to deny its maker?
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 8 form a woe oracle in which judgment turns suddenly into deliverance; the hinge comes in verse 5 with the words "suddenly, in an instant." Verses 9 to 24 are a series of shorter oracles on spiritual blindness that end in a promise of restoration. Images of sleep and dreaming tie the halves together: the attacking nations are like a hungry man who dreams of eating and wakes still hungry (verse 8), and the people of Jerusalem are under a spirit of deep sleep (verse 10). Reversals drive the second half. The wise lose their wisdom (verse 14), clay questions the potter (verse 16), Lebanon becomes an orchard (verse 17), and the deaf and blind receive hearing and sight (verse 18). The chapter closes with the name "the Holy One of Jacob" (verse 23), a variation on Isaiah's favorite title for God.

outline.t: Woe to Ariel: Jerusalem besieged and brought low
The attacking nations vanish like a dream
Spiritual blindness and the sealed book
Lip worship and the confounding of the wise
Woe to those who hide their plans: the potter and the clay
The deaf will hear, the blind will see, and Jacob will stand in awe

doctrines.note: The chapter contrasts external religion with real reverence. Worship made of "rules taught by men" (verse 13) is empty; the restored people will "sanctify the Holy One of Jacob" and stand in awe of him (verse 23).
The potter image in verse 16 makes God the maker who knows and rules what he has made. No plan hidden in the dark escapes him, and the attacking armies are in his hand.
God's word can be present yet closed to those who will not hear it (verses 11 and 12). Spiritual blindness is here both a judgment and a condition God promises to heal.

words.note: Ariel, a name used five times in this chapter for Jerusalem. The same form appears in Ezekiel 43:15-16 for the altar hearth, and verse 2 plays on that meaning. Some interpreters also hear lion of God in it. The name suggests that the city of sacrifice will itself become a place of burning.

Lev, heart. In Hebrew thought the heart is the center of thinking, choosing, and loyalty, not only of feeling. Verse 13's charge that the people's hearts are far from God means that their minds and wills are elsewhere even while their mouths say the right words.

Yatsar, to form, and as a participle, potter. The same verb is used in Genesis 2:7 when God forms the man from dust. In verse 16 Isaiah uses it to mock the idea that the formed thing could claim its maker has no understanding.

christ: Jesus quoted verse 13 against religious leaders who set aside God's command for the sake of their traditions (Matthew 15:7-9; Mark 7:6-7), following the Greek wording that says they worship in vain. Paul quotes verse 14 in 1 Corinthians 1:19 to show that God confounds human wisdom through the message of the cross, and the potter image of verse 16 lies behind his argument in Romans 9:20-21. The promise that the deaf will hear and the blind will see finds its most direct fulfillment in Jesus' healings, which he himself pointed to as evidence of who he was, in language drawn largely from Isaiah 35 and 61 (Matthew 11:4-5). The sealed book is also opened in Christ: the risen Jesus opened his disciples' minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45).

hard.q: If the LORD pours out a spirit of deep sleep on the people (verse 10), how can they be blamed for not seeing?
hard.a:
This is the same difficulty raised by Isaiah's commission in 6:9-10, where he is sent to make the people's ears dull. The text holds together two things: the people have already closed their own eyes (verse 9 says "blind yourselves"), and God confirms the blindness they have chosen as a judgment. Many interpreters describe this as judicial hardening, God handing people over to what they persistently prefer, as Paul describes in Romans 1:24-28.

The chapter does not leave it there. The same God who shuts eyes promises to open them (verse 18) and to bring the wayward to understanding (verse 24). Hardening in Isaiah serves a larger purpose of healing, a pattern Paul also sees in Romans 11, where Israel's partial hardening is not final.

questions: Verse 13 describes worship with the lips while the heart is far away. How can someone tell whether their own religious practice has become routine?
The planners in verse 15 thought no one saw them. Why do people try to keep parts of their lives hidden from God, and what does the potter image say about that?
The chapter promises that the humble and the poor will rejoice (verse 19). Why are they the first to receive what God is doing?
